opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that I never saw the distance as a reason not to start. If anything, it was the reason to start early.

When I was doing my PhD, and later when I came back to start my lab, most of my work was in 3D vision and embodied perception: how a machine can understand objects, their geometry, their pose, how they can be grasped and manipulated. At some point I realized that all of these questions converge on one ultimate scenario: a robot that can operate in an unstructured, everyday environment like a home. The home is the hardest test. Every household is different, objects are cluttered, lighting changes, people move around, and the tasks are long-horizon and open-ended. If you can solve the home, you've essentially solved general-purpose embodied intelligence.

So I didn't think of it as "home robots are coming next year, let's build a product." I thought of it as a north star. You set a goal that's far away, then you work backward and ask what capabilities are missing and which ones can be built step by step. Grasping arbitrary objects, for example, is a foundational skill. If a robot can't reliably pick up whatever is in front of it, nothing else matters. So we spent years on dexterous grasping, on synthetic data, on simulation-to-real transfer. Each of those is a stepping stone that's useful on its own, even before the full home robot exists.

The other thing is that I believe in the data and simulation route. Real-world robot data is extremely expensive to collect, and you can't scale it the way language models scaled with internet text. So a big part of our thinking was: can we generate massive amounts of high-quality synthetic data in simulation, train models that generalize, and then transfer them to real robots? That approach makes a far-off goal more tractable, because you aren't waiting for millions of robots to be deployed before you have enough data.

And practically, you don't have to go straight into homes. There are intermediate scenarios like retail, pharmacies, factories, and warehouses that are more structured but still require general manipulation skills. You can create real value there, generate revenue, collect feedback, and keep iterating toward the harder setting. So the path is home as the destination, with commercially viable stops along the way.

Finally, there's a timing element. With large models and generative AI, the brain side of robotics suddenly got much stronger. Robots can now understand instructions, reason about tasks, and plan in ways that weren't possible five years ago. That shifted my estimate of how far away the goal really is. It's still far, but it no longer feels like science fiction. It feels like an engineering and scientific problem that a determined team can push forward. That's what made me decide it was worth committing to.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the distance from practical realization was a reason to start early. It does not attribute unwillingness to invest to Kai-Fu Lee.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes PhD and lab research as steps toward home robotics, then mentions commercial opportunities along the way. It does not present academic research as continuing until the time is ripe to move into industry.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I started, I didn't think of it as "pursuing home robots." I thought of it as pursuing the problems that stand between us and home robots, and those problems were worth solving on their own terms.

Back around 2017, 2018, if you looked at what robots could actually do, it was pretty humbling. A robot could pick up a known object in a lab, in fixed lighting, from a fixed pose. Change the object, change the clutter, change the viewpoint, and it would fail. So the gap between that and a robot that walks into your kitchen and puts away the dishes was enormous. Anyone who said "five years" was either selling something or hadn't tried it.

But I had a strong belief, which came out of my time working on 3D vision and later in Leonidas Guibas's group, that the bottleneck wasn't mechanical. The hardware was already decent. The bottleneck was perception and understanding. A robot doesn't fail at grasping because its fingers are bad. It fails because it doesn't really know what it's looking at: where the object is, how it's oriented, where you can hold it, how it will move once you touch it. Those are vision problems. And vision was exactly the field where deep learning was starting to make things that seemed impossible become routine.

So my thinking was: if the end state is far away, then the right thing to do is to pick the layer of the stack that is both fundamental and unsolved, and go deep on it. For me that was 3D understanding of objects for manipulation: category-level pose estimation, articulated objects, generalizable grasping. These are things you need for a home robot no matter what the final architecture looks like. If I'm wrong about the timeline, the work still matters. If I'm right, I've built the foundation.

There's also a more personal answer. I think young researchers are often told to work on things that will "land" quickly, and I understand why. But the problems that are five or ten years out are where you can actually define the agenda rather than follow it. When I came back to Peking University, I chose embodied AI precisely because almost nobody around me was betting on it. It felt risky, and it was. But I'd rather spend a decade on a hard problem I believe in than two years on an easy one I don't.

And frankly, the field moved faster than I expected. Large models changed what's possible in reasoning and language grounding, simulation got good enough to generate data at scale, and suddenly things we treated as long-term research became engineering questions. I don't think home robots are here yet. But I no longer think "far away" means what it meant when I started.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention Kai-Fu Lee or attribute anyone’s unwillingness to invest in home robots to their distance from practical realization.

r002.rationale: The response describes choosing academic research on embodied AI, but does not present it as a way to pursue home robotics until the timing is right to move into industry.

astra-6.text:
For me, the fact that home robots were still far away didn’t mean they weren’t worth pursuing. It meant we had to separate the long-term goal from the problems we could actually work on. A robot in a home has to deal with unfamiliar objects, changing environments, and people doing things it hasn’t anticipated. Those are fundamental challenges.

So I thought about it as a direction for research, rather than a product we could deliver immediately. Could we make progress on perception? Could we help a robot understand how to interact with an object? Each step could be useful on its own while bringing us closer to the larger goal. You don’t have to know exactly when the whole thing will become practical, but you do need a concrete next problem to solve.

r001.rationale: The response says home robots were far from practical and still worth pursuing, but it does not attribute anyone’s unwillingness to invest to that distance or mention Kai-Fu Lee.

r002.rationale: It frames home robotics as a research direction with useful incremental problems, but does not present academic research as a bridge to entering industry when the time is ripe.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the fact that home robots were still far away was part of what made the problem worth pursuing. If you imagine a robot helping someone at home, you quickly realize how much it needs to understand: the space, the objects, what the person wants, and how to act safely when things don’t go exactly as expected.

I didn’t think we had to solve all of that at once. The question was: what can we work on today that moves us toward that goal? You can keep a long-term vision while choosing concrete problems where you can make progress and learn. That was how I thought about it—take the ambition seriously, but be very practical about the next step.

r001.rationale: The response says home robots being far from practical use made the problem worth pursuing, but it does not mention Kai-Fu Lee or attribute an unwillingness to invest to him.
